solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Total cancellation of debt

blocks.note: first meaning: to wreck a vehicle beyond repair, as insurers say
second meaning: an accounting entry that clears a sum that will never be paid

explanation.surface: Someone longs for every debt they owe to be wiped out completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Total' reads as an adjective qualifying the cancellation, but it is a verb standing on its own, as in totalling a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase serves as a verb for destroying a vehicle and as a noun for a bad loan formally abandoned in the accounts.

clue.text: Our meal composed of French creamy sauce

indicators.note: to compose is to put together or arrange, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: letters taken as written for rearranging
de is the French word for of

explanation.surface: A diner describes a dinner made entirely of French dishes, with a creamy sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed of' looks like one phrase meaning made from; it splits into the rearranging signal and a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rémoulade is a mayonnaise-based condiment from French cookery, often served with celeriac or fish.

clue.text: Browned off for a start, tried going outside

indicators.note: a start is the beginning, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
to go outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: to try food is to taste it
first letter of off

explanation.surface: Someone fed up at the outset still tried going out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browned off' is British slang for fed up and reads as one phrase; the definition is only 'Browned', and 'off' supplies its first letter. O goes inside TASTED to make TOASTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread that has been toasted has been browned under heat, so the two past participles are synonyms.

clue.text: Welsh girl taking fresh look around

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: fresh means new
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A young woman from Wales tries out a new appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh look' suggests a makeover; the two words simply give NEW and LO, and together they turn backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Olwen is a traditional Welsh female name, borne by the heroine of the medieval tale of Culhwch and Olwen.

clue.text: Hairstyle cut at front and back

indicators.note: cutting at the front trims off the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: an Afro is a rounded, bushy hairstyle

explanation.surface: A barber trims a hairstyle at both the front and the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front and back' looks like a pair describing where the cut goes; 'back' is actually the definition, as in to and fro.
explanation.definitionFit: In the phrase to and fro, the second word means away or backwards, so it stands for back in the opposite direction.

clue.text: Flirt? Mademoiselle’s that, in bed

indicators.note: one thing lying in another is enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
a French young lady would say que for that

explanation.surface: Is a young Frenchwoman a flirt? Apparently so, in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The saucy suggestion hides a language convention: Mademoiselle marks a French word, and 'that' in French is que.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, coquet means to trifle with affections or dally amorously, the same behaviour as flirting.

clue.text: Shoddy hat worn by man given lift

indicators.note: something worn by a person goes round them, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: a cap is a kind of hat
he is the pronoun for a man
a jack lifts a car to change a wheel

explanation.surface: A man in a tatty hat is offered a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given lift' sounds like being offered a ride, but it adds the car-raising tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapjack describes goods that are inferior and badly made, originally from pedlars selling tawdry wares.

clue.text: Group extremely exuberant after a couple of pints

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outside letters are kept
coming after something means following it, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: a quart is two pints
first and last letters of exuberant

explanation.surface: A band gets very lively after a couple of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely exuberant' reads as very lively; 'extremely' actually keeps just the ends. 'after' places those letters behind the measure of two pints.
explanation.definitionFit: A quartet is a set of four performers or items, a specific kind of group.

clue.text: Half of them object to change

indicators.note: half of a word means just part of its letters, here the second pair

blocks.note: the back half of the four-letter word
an end is an aim or object

explanation.surface: Half the group raise objections to making changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'object' looks like a verb meaning protest; it is a noun meaning purpose, which gives END.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to alter a text by correcting it, so it is a specific kind of making changes.

clue.text: Work repulsing American setter

indicators.note: to repulse is to drive back, so the letters are sent the other way

blocks.note: Am is the abbreviation for American
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: A job is driving away a dog breed from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' suggests a dog, but in crosswords it is the compiler, so ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is a novel by Jane Austen, so it is an example of a literary work.

clue.text: Jam and salt picked up … from this trader?

indicators.note: to pick up can mean to hear, so what we need is how the words are heard

blocks.note: being in a hole is being in a jam
an old salt is a seasoned seaman

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether preserves and salt were bought from this merchant.
explanation.walkthrough: The groceries suggest a shop; jam is a difficulty (a hole), and a salt is a sailor. Said together, they sound like the merchant.
explanation.definitionFit: A wholesaler is a merchant who sells goods in bulk to retailers, a particular kind of trader.

clue.text: Unrelaxed, yet in shape after exercise?

blocks.note: yet and but are both conjunctions of contrast
exercise tones up the body

explanation.surface: Someone is tense, even though they are fit after working out.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma looks like a break between two clauses, but the whole second part builds the answer from a conjunction and a fitness phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Buttoned-up describes a person who is reserved and inhibited, unable to loosen or show feelings.

clue.text: Divisional leader wants support of course, guarding RAF conscript

indicators.note: the leader is whoever goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept
to guard something is to stand round it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: first letter of Divisional
taken as written
on a golf course, the ball is supported on a tee

explanation.surface: A divisional commander naturally wants backing for guarding an air force recruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' sounds like 'naturally', but it points to a golf course, where the small peg is a support. D and TEE together surround RAF.
explanation.definitionFit: A draftee is someone called up for compulsory military service, the American word for a conscript.

clue.text: Recurrent spot of bother

blocks.note: surface reading: a small problem that keeps coming back
setter's reading: the fuss is written as a two-letter chunk and then a near-repeat of it, each ending in O

explanation.walkthrough: A 'spot of bother' is British understatement for a bit of trouble; the word for such a fuss has two halves that echo each other, which is what 'Recurrent' hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is a commotion or fuss, the kind of minor trouble the British call a spot of bother.

clue.text: A right noise in centre of Asian island

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so the outer letters are dropped
a thing placed in another is enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
a din is a loud noise
the middle three letters of Asian

explanation.surface: There is a real racket in the middle of an island in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asian island' reads as one phrase, but 'Asian' is only fodder; the island is Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: Sardinia is a large Italian island in the Mediterranean, an example of an island.

clue.text: Publication of pay finally accepted by Tyneside labourer

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
something accepted is taken in, so this piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in the North East of England, abbreviated NE
a labourer is a worker
last letter of pay

explanation.surface: A labourer in Newcastle accepts the published details of his wages.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside is the area round Newcastle upon Tyne in north-east England, a region crosswords abbreviate by its compass points. 'Publication' at the front looks like it governs 'of pay', but it stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Yorker is a long-running American weekly magazine, an example of a publication.

clue.text: Arranged seat with sailors at back of ship

indicators.note: arranging things puts them into a new order, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: letters taken as written for rearranging
RN is the Royal Navy, a crossword standard for sailors

explanation.surface: A seat has been set out for the crew at the rear of the vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole nautical phrase at the end is the definition, which suits an adverb answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is an adverb meaning behind or towards the rear of a vessel, the stern end.

clue.text: Acquiring information at university, after fearing missing first

indicators.note: missing the first means losing the opening letter
coming after something means following it, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: fearing is dreading, which loses its opening D
a British student in residence is said to be up at university

explanation.surface: A nervous student studies at university after worrying about missing out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the start and runs over the comma-free phrase, so 'at university' looks like part of it; it is the UP.
explanation.definitionFit: To read up on a subject is to study it intensively, gaining knowledge about it.

clue.text: Brief dog-like whine, base and cowardly

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a yelp is a dog's short cry, curtailed here
base and low both mean mean-spirited

explanation.surface: Someone is dismissed as a whimpering, contemptible coward.
explanation.walkthrough: The list of insults reads as three descriptions; only the last is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is informal slang for lacking courage, the colour traditionally linked with fear.

clue.text: Alpine transport loaded with funny cases

indicators.note: a vehicle loaded with things holds them inside

blocks.note: a luge is a small toboggan used in the Alps
a funny is a joke, and so is a gag

explanation.surface: A mountain vehicle is piled high with odd-looking suitcases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' seems to describe the cases, but it is a noun meaning a joke. 'cases' is the definition, not part of the load.
explanation.definitionFit: Suitcases and bags are a traveller's baggage, so cases collectively make up the answer.

clue.text: About to go, ordered the attack with such belligerent words?

indicators.note: something that is to go is to be removed
to order things is to put them in a new sequence

blocks.note: C stands for circa, about, and is the letter removed
letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A commander on the point of leaving orders an assault, shouting defiance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to go' reads as 'ready to leave'; C (circa) leaves the letters of THE ATTACK, and the rest is reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation accompanies a blow or triumph, typical defiant language hurled at an opponent.

clue.text: Travellers initially go astray again, dodging western rocky area

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter counts
to dodge something is to avoid it, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: first letter of Travellers
to err is to wander from the right path
anew means again
W is the abbreviation for western, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Travellers get lost once more while avoiding a rough western landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'western' seems to describe the rocky area, but it is W, removed from ANEW.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology a terrane is a fault-bounded crustal block with its own distinct rock history.

clue.text: Good former service for women? The reverse, for men

indicators.note: the reverse of a thing is its back-to-front version, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
the ATS was the Auxiliary Territorial Service, Britain's women's army branch in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Something good was once available for women; the opposite applies for men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for women' looks like the definition's partner to 'for men', but it belongs to the old army service. A stag night is a British men-only party before a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Stag is an adjective for events restricted to males, as in a stag party or stag night.

clue.text: Train apprentices principally in college

indicators.note: principally means chiefly or first of all, so only the opening letter is kept
one thing in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: a tech is a technical college
first letter of apprentices

explanation.surface: Apprentices are trained mainly at college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like a verb acting on the apprentices; it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To teach someone is to instruct them in a skill, so it is a synonym of the verb train.

clue.text: Stress concerning Southern transport

blocks.note: over can mean about or concerning
S is the abbreviation for southern
a train is a means of transport

explanation.surface: Commuters worry about the reliability of Southern rail services.
explanation.walkthrough: Southern is a British rail operator notorious for delays, so the surface suggests commuter anxiety; it gives only S.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstrain is to put excessive tension or effort on something, which is to stress it.

clue.text: Asparagus portion, small, served with avocado?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
the avocado is also known as the avocado pear

explanation.surface: A small helping of asparagus arrives alongside some avocado.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that avocado is defined by example: its other name is avocado pear.
explanation.definitionFit: A single shoot of asparagus is called a spear, from its long pointed shape.

clue.text: Soda maker’s horrendous bloomer

indicators.note: something horrendous is a dreadful mess, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: letters taken as written, the S included

explanation.surface: A drinks manufacturer has made an awful mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' is British slang for a blunder, which fits the surface; here it means a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The damask rose is a fragrant old rose variety grown for attar, so it is something that blooms.

clue.text: No opening for idle dunce

indicators.note: with no opening, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: to loaf is to idle about

explanation.surface: There is no job vacancy for a lazy dimwit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No opening' sounds like no job available; it drops the first letter of the verb for idling.
explanation.definitionFit: An oaf is a clumsy, stupid person, so it works as a synonym for a dullard.

clue.text: Final parts of regular journey for old ship

indicators.note: the final parts of a word are its closing letters, so only the tail is kept

blocks.note: the last two letters of regular
to go is to travel or make a journey

explanation.surface: The last stages of a routine voyage for a veteran vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final parts' suggests last letters of several words; it takes the closing pair of 'regular' only.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo was the legendary vessel of Jason and the Argonauts in Greek mythology.

clue.text: It’s a pity organ accompanies spoken verse

indicators.note: spoken means said out loud, so we want the sound not the spelling
to accompany is to go alongside, so the two pieces sit next to each other

blocks.note: an ode is a lyric poem
the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: Sadly, the organ music plays alongside a poetry recital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' suggests music, but it is a body part. The short poem, said aloud, is split as 'oh' plus D.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation expresses mild regret or dismay, the same feeling as saying something is a shame.

clue.text: Purpose of crenellations, maybe indefinitely

blocks.note: first meaning, whimsical: battlements are built on castle towers
second meaning: permanently, with no end in sight

explanation.surface: A historian wonders what castle battlements were for, and for how long.
explanation.walkthrough: A keep is the main tower of a castle, and crenellations are the notched battlements on top, so they exist for keeps; 'maybe' flags the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means permanently or for good, with no time limit on possession.
